issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should order the institution of criminal action based on the material on record.

facts: The Court found that the initial police investigation into the matter was "desultory and lackadaisical," suffering from "casualness, lack of incisiveness and unreasonable dilatoriness."
The investigation of the case had been transferred from the local police to the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) at the petitioner's request.
application: The Supreme Court reviewed the material on record and determined that it did not justify a direct order from the Court to institute a criminal action.
The Court stated, "we do not think that on the material before us we can go that far."
Instead of ordering a criminal action itself, the Court deferred to the ongoing investigative process.
It directed the CBI to complete its investigation within three months and then "take such action as may be warranted by the result of the investigation."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the request to order the institution of a criminal action because it found the material on record was insufficient to justify such an order. Instead, it directed the CBI to complete its investigation and take appropriate action based on its findings.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should determine if the death was a suicide or a murder.

application.text: The Supreme Court explicitly stated that it was not possible, nor would it be right, for it to decide the question of whether the death was a suicide or a murder.
The Court reasoned that this determination is a matter that should be properly handled during the trial of a criminal charge by a court that possesses the appropriate jurisdiction.

The Court clarified that its discussion of the case's features was not for the purpose of determining the cause of death, but rather to draw attention to the manner in which the police investigation was conducted.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the issue, deciding that the determination of whether the death was a suicide or murder is a function of the trial court with criminal jurisdiction, not the Supreme Court in this proceeding.

issue.issue_text: Whether the investigation of the case should be transferred to the C.B.I.

facts: The Court found that the initial police investigation was "desultory and lackadaisical," and suffered from "casualness, lack of incisiveness and unreasonable dilatoriness."
There was a suggestion that the police were reluctant to pursue the investigation vigorously to avoid embarrassing one of the families involved.
The case was passed between multiple police officers who were already overburdened with numerous other cases.
The police failed to promptly secure evidence, such as not seizing a blanket used to put out the fire and waiting over five weeks for a forensic report on fingerprints.
Crucial witnesses, including the taxi driver who took the victim to the hospital and a person who was first on the scene, were not questioned.
The police's own Crime Branch considered the investigation to be "materially inadequate."
reasoning.conclusion: Based on the numerous and significant failures of the police, the Court concluded that their investigation did not inspire confidence. As a result, it accepted the petitioner's request and ordered the investigation to be transferred to the C.B.I. to ensure a proper and effective inquiry into the case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should order the institution of criminal action based on the material on record.
appellant_arguments: The investigating agency did not carry out its statutory duties in a bonafide manner.
The agency deliberately delayed the investigation to ensure that no proceedings were taken against the accused.
There are several suspicious circumstances in the case.
The opinion of the C.F.S.L. experts was assailed.
respondent_arguments: The material on record is not sufficient to warrant an order from the Supreme Court directing the institution of criminal action.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should determine if the death was a suicide or a murder.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's arguments pointing to suspicious circumstances, bad faith by the investigating agency, and questionable expert opinions were intended to establish that a crime (murder) had been committed.
respondent_arguments: The determination of the cause of death is a matter for the investigating agency, which is now the C.B.I., and not for the Supreme Court to decide in the present proceedings.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the investigation of the case should be transferred to the C.B.I.
appellant_arguments: The investigating agency did not carry out its statutory duties in a bonafide manner.
The agency deliberately withheld filing a police report and delayed the investigation to protect the accused.
respondent_arguments: The investigation of the case was already transferred by the Minister of State for Home Affairs to the Central Bureau of Investigation on September 11, 1981.
Because the case was transferred to the C.B.I., no question arose of the Delhi police filing any report under s. 173(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A court cannot order the institution of criminal action if the material on record is insufficient to justify such an order.
obiter: Entries in a police Case Diary must be made with promptness, in sufficient detail, mentioning all significant facts, in careful chronological order and with complete objectivity.
The greed for dowry and the dowry system as an institution calls for the severest condemnation, as legislative measures alone have not succeeded in stamping out this evil.
The application of the Coroners' Act, 1871 should be extended to more cities to make inquiries into deaths more meaningful and effective.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: While the Court found the material on record insufficient to directly order the institution of criminal action, and determined it was not its proper role to decide if the death was a suicide or murder, it concluded that the police investigation was seriously flawed. The haphazard maintenance of the police Case Diary defeated its purpose and cast doubt on the bonafides of the investigation, justifying the transfer of the case to the C.B.I. for a proper and timely conclusion.
legal_tests_applied: The standard for maintaining a police Case Diary, which requires that entries be made with 'promptness, in sufficient detail, mentioning all significant facts, in careful chronological order and with complete objectivity.'

The jurisdictional principle that the Supreme Court should not determine factual questions of guilt (e.g., suicide vs. murder), as that is a matter 'properly involved in the trial of a criminal charge by a court possessing jurisdiction.'
why_appellant_lost: Regarding the institution of criminal action, the Court concluded that 'the material on record does not, however, justify an order to that effect by the Court.'

Regarding the determination of whether the death was a suicide or murder, the Court stated, 'It is not possible, in this case, nor indeed would it be right for the Court to do so, to enter into the question... That is a matter which is properly involved in the trial of a criminal charge by a court possessing jurisdiction.'
why_respondent_won: The Court agreed that the evidence presented was not sufficient for it to order a prosecution, stating 'we do not think that on the material before us we can go that far.'
The Court affirmed the jurisdictional boundary that it is not the proper forum to make a factual determination on the cause of death, which is a matter for a trial court.
policy_considerations: The Court condemned the 'greed for dowry' and the dowry system as a 'deep·seated malady in- our social order' and noted the failure of legislative measures like the Dowry Prohibition Act to stamp out the evil.

The Court emphasized the systemic importance of proper police work, stating, 'We think it to be of the utmost importance that the entries in a police Case Diary should be made with promptness, in sufficient detail, mentioning all significant facts, in careful chronological order and with complete objectivity.'

The Court observed that the death of a young wife in such circumstances must be attributed 'either to the commission of a crime or to the fact that, mentally tortured by the suffocating circumstances surrounding her, she committed suicide.'
